question: An otherwise healthy 31-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a several-day history of sharp, central chest pain, which is constant and unrelated to exertion. The pain gets worse on lying down and decreases with sitting forward. He has smoked 10–15 cigarettes daily for the past 7 years. His blood pressure is 120/50 mm Hg, the pulse is 92/min, and the temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F). On physical examination, a scratching sound is heard at end-expiration with the patient leaning forward. ECG is shown in the image. Serum troponin is mildly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? ?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Smoking -> Increased risk of cardiovascular disease -> Chest pain presentation -> 80% CHAIN: Chest pain worsens on lying down -> Relieved by sitting forward -> Suggestive of pericarditis -> 85% CHAIN: Scratching sound at end-expiration -> Pericardial friction rub -> Classic finding in acute pericarditis -> 90% CHAIN: Mildly elevated troponin -> Suggestive of myocardial involvement in pericarditis -> 85% CHAIN: ECG showing diffuse ST-segment elevation -> Consistent with acute pericarditis -> 95% CHAIN: Diagnosis most likely acute pericarditis -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 31-year-old man with central chest pain worsened by lying down and relieved by sitting forward, along with a scratching sound at end-expiration and mildly elevated troponin, is acute pericarditis. This is supported by the ECG showing diffuse ST-segment elevation, which is consistent with acute pericarditis. The evidence paths linking the ECG findings to chest pain and acute pericarditis further reinforce this diagnosis.
analysis: The core medical principle here is to consider the clinical presentation, physical exam findings, and ECG changes to arrive at a diagnosis. In this case, the patient's symptoms of central chest pain worsened by lying down and relieved by sitting forward, along with the physical exam finding of a scratching sound at end-expiration and the ECG showing diffuse ST-segment elevation, are highly suggestive of acute pericarditis. The patient's smoking history and age also make this diagnosis more likely than other options. Acute pericarditis is characterized by inflammation of the pericardium, leading to chest pain that is typically pleuritic and positional, as seen in this patient.
